newsitem.title: USA: White House officials booed on welfare law.
newsitem.headline: White House officials booed on welfare law.

text.p: A top White House official got a personal taste of anger brewing over a new welfare law Monday when he was booed by activists who chanted "a day's work for a day's pay" and compared some public work programmes to slavery.

Gene Sperling, director of the National Economic Council, got a testy reception when he spoke to a meeting of ACORN, the Association of Community Organisations for Reform Now, at a church just blocks from the Capitol.

Sperling defended President Clinton's decision to sign the welfare law and said the White House would not agree to any balanced budget deal that did not restore some spending cuts in programmes for the poor.
"He is a president whose heart is in the right place, who wants to do the right thing," Sperling said.
"There is no question that there were things in that welfare bill that they were not only bad policy, they were unconscionable, they were wrong," he said.
Sperling fielded questions, flanked by signs reading "Welfare Workers Union Yes!" and "President Clean Clean Up This Welfare Mess."
The chanting audience in the pews included hundreds of people required to pick up trash or participate in other public works jobs to earn public assistance.

Participants asked whether the White House supported their efforts to unionize and ensure minimum wage laws applied to "workfare." Sperling said those issues were under review but the "overall orientation" was to see the laws applied broadly.
Workfare is a practice of working for welfare benefits.
A Brooklyn minister warned a pending cutoff of benefits to legal immigrants under the law was causing great fear.

"The cuts in benfits to immigrants, the cuts to Food Stamps have a devastating impact on our community ... the sense of hopelessness has risen to an alarming degree and I am terribly afraid what the repercussions will be," the minister said.
Others complained they were required to perform menial or dangerous tasks in workfare programmes and received little training. Several compared such work to slavery.
Sperling was booed, but also applauded when he reminded the crowd Clinton had pushed for universal health care and was working to restore cuts in the welfare bill.

He promised more open communication, remarking that Clinton -- who ran into flak during a recent roundtable discussion of welfare in New York -- would have liked to address the group if he had not been sidelined with an injured knee.
